exact_query: why do cross-border b2b payouts fail
raw_response:
Cross-border B2B payouts fail or experience severe delays for a variety of technical, regulatory, and operational reasons. Unlike domestic transactions—which typically use unified local clearing houses—international B2B payments must navigate multi-layered networks, distinct national banking systems, and rigorous compliance checks.

The primary reasons cross-border B2B payouts fail can be categorized into six core areas:

### 1. Incorrect or Incomplete Beneficiary Data

This is the most common cause of immediate rejections and automated returns.

* **Data Mismatches:** A single mistyped character in an IBAN, a wrong SWIFT/BIC code, an outdated routing number, or an invalid account format will cause automated bank systems to reject the transfer.
* **Name Mismatch:** Many receiving banks enforce strict automated name-matching. If the company name on the payout instruction does not precisely match the legal business name registered on the bank account (e.g., missing a "LLC," "GmbH," or handling punctuation differently), the payment is frequently paused or returned.

### 2. Compliance, Sanctions, and AML Screening (RFIs)

Cross-border payments face intense regulatory scrutiny under Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) laws.

* **Sanctions & Watchlists:** Transactions that trigger automated flags against global sanctions lists, politically exposed persons (PEPs), or high-risk jurisdictions are frozen or blocked.
* **Requests for Information (RFIs):** If the purpose of payment is vague (e.g., missing invoice numbers or clear descriptions), intermediary or receiving banks will halt the transaction and issue an RFI. If the parties fail to respond quickly, the payment defaults or is returned.

### 3. Intermediary Bank (Correspondent Banking) Friction

Very few international B2B payments move directly from the sender’s bank to the receiver’s bank. They typically rely on a chain of **correspondent/intermediary banks**.

* **Chain Vulnerability:** Each intermediary bank in the chain processes the payment independently, applies its own compliance screening, and has its own technical formatting rules. If *any* bank in the chain encounters an issue or uses a stricter risk policy, the entire payment can be rejected or delayed.

### 4. Currency Conversion and Liquidity Issues

B2B transactions often involve moving funds from one currency to another (FX), creating opportunities for failure.

* **Insufficient Funds or Mismatched Currencies:** If the sending account lacks sufficient funds to cover the principal amount *plus* fluctuating foreign exchange spreads, intermediary fees, and destination charges, the payment will be rejected.
* **Liquidity Locks:** If a local currency lacks market liquidity or has strict capital controls (common in certain emerging markets), payouts can be indefinitely delayed or blocked by local central banks.

### 5. Cut-Off Times and Time Zone Misalignments

Timing discrepancies frequently disrupt international transfers.

* **Missed Windows:** If a payment instruction is submitted after a bank’s daily processing **cut-off time**, or crosses over weekends and public holidays in the destination country, it sits idle.
* **Extended Settlement Lags:** Because different countries operate on different business calendars, a payout might appear "sent" locally while effectively sitting frozen in a clearing queue across a different time zone.

### 6. Technical Formatting and Rail Incompatibilities

* **Outdated Message Formats:** Traditional rails like SWIFT have been undergoing massive migration toward the **ISO 20022** XML data standard. If an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system or legacy platform exports payment instructions in an incompatible or corrupted format, parsing errors occur at the receiving end.
* **Unsupported Corridors:** Attempting to send a payout via a rail that does not support the specific account type (e.g., trying to route a commercial payout through a consumer-only channel) results in an automatic system rejection.

[stripe](https://stripe.com/resources/more/cross-border-b2b-payments-a-guide-for-businesses) |

## Why B2B makes it harder

B2B payments carry more required context than consumer payments: invoices, purchase orders, tax identifiers, payment purposes, and internal approvals. Missing or inconsistent data can trigger compliance reviews or make reconciliation impossible even when the funds eventually arrive. [stripe](https://stripe.com/resources/more/cross-border-b2b-payments-a-guide-for-businesses)

Cross-border payments also tend to be a “black box”: the sender often cannot see which intermediaries touched the payment, where it is stuck, what fees were deducted, or when the beneficiary bank will post it. [paypal](https://www.paypal.com/us/brc/article/what-are-cross-border-payouts-and-its-challenges)

## The most preventable failures

Most operational failures come down to data and process hygiene:

- Validate IBANs, account numbers, BICs, routing numbers, and beneficiary names before submission.
- Collect complete KYB/KYC information before onboarding a recipient, especially for first-time or high-value payouts.
- Use clear, specific payment references and purpose codes where local rules require them.
- Pre-fund the correct currency account and monitor balances before batch runs.
- Build idempotency, retry logic, webhook/status tracking, and exception queues into the payout workflow.
- Quote the full recipient amount—including FX and intermediary fees—rather than treating fees as an afterthought. [stripe](https://stripe.com/resources/more/cross-border-payouts-strategies-for-faster-more-reliable-global-payments)

## A useful distinction

A payout can “fail” in two different ways: it may be **rejected before settlement**, or it may **settle but reach the recipient short, late, or without usable remittance data**. The second case is especially damaging in B2B because finance teams then have to manually match an unexplained bank credit to invoices, orders, and deductions. [sunrate](https://www.sunrate.com/blog/globalpayment/what-b2b-marketplaces-need-from-cross-border-payout-infrastructure/)

In short: cross-border B2B payouts fail less because money movement is inherently impossible and more because fragmented rails, compliance controls, incomplete data, and opaque intermediary economics create many silent points of failure. exact_query: why do cross-border b2b payouts fail
raw_response:
Cross-border B2B payouts fail when money cannot successfully move from a business in one country to a business or beneficiary in another due to issues with payment information, banking infrastructure, compliance checks, currency conversion, or intermediary banks.

The important thing is that a payout can fail at multiple stages of the payment journey, not just at the receiving bank.

## 1. The 8 main reasons cross-border B2B payouts fail

### 1. Incorrect beneficiary details

- Wrong account number, IBAN, or SWIFT/BIC code.
- Incorrect beneficiary name or address.
- Missing bank branch or routing information.
- Mismatch between the registered company name and account holder.

Impact: The receiving bank rejects or returns the payment.

### 2. Regulatory and compliance restrictions

- AML (Anti-Money Laundering) checks.
- Sanctions screening.
- Missing KYC/KYB documentation.
- Unclear source of funds.
- Payments involving restricted countries or entities.

Impact: Payments are held, delayed, rejected, or frozen for investigation.

### 3. Intermediary bank failures

Cross-border payments often pass through multiple correspondent banks.

- An intermediary bank doesn't support the payment currency.
- A correspondent banking relationship has been terminated.
- An intermediary rejects the transaction.
- Payment instructions are lost or incorrectly interpreted.

Impact: Funds get stuck in transit or returned to the sender.

### 4. Currency conversion problems

- Unsupported currency pairs.
- Insufficient liquidity.
- Exchange-rate volatility.
- Unexpected conversion fees.
- Incorrect settlement currency.

Impact: Payments fail, settle for an unexpected amount, or take longer than expected.

### 5. Insufficient funds or liquidity

- The sending business has insufficient funds.
- The payment provider lacks prefunded balances.
- Liquidity is unavailable in the destination currency.
- Funding accounts have not been replenished.

Impact: The payout cannot be executed or settled.

### 6. Payment network and infrastructure issues

- SWIFT network disruptions.
- Local clearing system downtime.
- Bank holidays and weekends.
- Payment gateway or API failures.
- Unsupported payment rails.

Impact: Payments are delayed, rejected, or left pending.

### 7. Country-specific banking requirements

Different countries have different payment requirements.

For example:

- India may require specific beneficiary and purpose-of-payment information.
- Brazil may require local tax and beneficiary information.
- China may impose additional documentation and foreign-exchange controls.
- European payments may require valid IBAN and beneficiary information.

Impact: A payment that works in one country may fail in another.

### 8. Technical and reconciliation failures

- API timeouts.
- Duplicate payment requests.
- Incorrect payment status updates.
- Webhook delivery failures.
- Missing transaction references.
- Mismatched settlement and reconciliation records.

Impact: The payout may be successful at the bank level but appear failed or pending in the payment platform.

## 2. Where do failures happen in the payout journey?

## Cross-border B2B payout flow

1. Business initiates payout
   Incorrect payment instructions, insufficient funds.
2. Payment provider processes transaction
   API errors, validation failures, duplicate requests.
3. Compliance and risk screening
   KYC/KYB, AML, sanctions screening, missing documents.
4. FX conversion and liquidity
   Insufficient liquidity, unsupported currency, FX issues.
5. Correspondent/intermediary banking
   Intermediary rejection, routing problems, missing relationships.
6. Beneficiary bank receives payment
   Account mismatch, local restrictions, bank rejection.
7. Settlement and reconciliation
   Delayed confirmation, missing references, status mismatches.

## 3. Business impact of failed payouts

| Stakeholder | Business impact |
| --- | --- |
| Payout sender | Operational costs and delayed obligations |
| Payment provider | Higher support costs and lower margins |
| Receiving business | Cash-flow disruptions |
| Suppliers | Delayed payments and damaged relationships |
| Finance teams | Manual reconciliation and investigation |
| Platform/marketplace | Reduced trust and customer retention |

## 4. How can payment providers reduce payout failures?

| Problem | Potential solution |
| --- | --- |
| Incorrect beneficiary details | Account validation before payout |
| Compliance failures | Pre-screening and automated KYB |
| Intermediary bank issues | Multiple banking and routing partners |
| FX liquidity shortages | Local currency liquidity management |
| Payment rail failures | Alternative local payment rails |
| Technical failures | Idempotency, retries and monitoring |
| Reconciliation issues | Real-time payment tracking and status updates |

## 5. The biggest underlying problem

In many cross-border B2B payout systems, the challenge is not simply moving money. It is coordinating multiple independent financial institutions, payment networks, compliance requirements, currencies, and settlement processes.

Three particularly important operational metrics are:

- Payout success rate: Percentage of initiated payouts successfully completed.
- First-time-right rate: Percentage of payouts completed without manual intervention or correction.
- Time to resolution: Time required to resolve failed, rejected, or stuck payouts.

A provider should also distinguish between technical failures, compliance holds, bank rejections, and returned payments. They require different solutions.

## 6. A useful way to think about this problem

If you're looking at this from a fintech, payments infrastructure, or B2B payments business perspective, I'd break the problem into three layers:

1. Payment initiation failure: The payment cannot be correctly created or funded.
2. Payment execution failure: The money cannot successfully travel through the banking network.
3. Payment confirmation failure: The money moves, but the provider cannot reliably confirm or reconcile the outcome.

This distinction is important because fixing API reliability alone won't solve intermediary bank rejections or compliance-related failures.

The key question is whether you're trying to understand this problem from a fintech product perspective, a payment operations perspective, or a business opportunity perspective. Each leads to a different set of insights.

exact_query: why do embedded finance platforms fail kyb onboarding
raw_response:
Embedded finance platforms often struggle with Know Your Business (KYB) onboarding due to a fundamental tension: **SaaS and digital platforms prioritize frictionless, instant user flows**, while **partner financial institutions (banks, issuers, payment processors) enforce strict regulatory risk standards**.

Unlike consumer onboarding (KYC), verifying a business requires validating complex corporate structures, multi-layered ownership chains, regulatory registries, and individual decision-makers.

The main reasons embedded finance platforms fail at KYB onboarding include:

---

### 1. High Friction vs. UX Expectations (Drop-Off Rate)

* **Excessive Document Requests:** Platforms frequently ask business owners to scan and upload official articles of incorporation, tax forms, and utility bills manually, rather than pulling from public registries programmatically.
* **The "UBO Bottleneck":** To fulfill anti-money laundering (AML) rules, platforms must identify and run identity checks on all Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBOs—typically anyone holding $\ge 25\%$ equity) and executive directors. If one co-founder or investor delays completing their individual check, the entire company’s application stalls indefinitely.

### 2. Manual Reviews & Operational Backlogs

* **Over-Reliance on Manual Verification:** Many platforms launch embedded fintech features using ad-hoc, manual operational workflows (e.g., analysts reviewing uploaded PDFs in email inboxes). As applicant volumes scale, review times balloon from minutes to weeks, leading applicants to abandon the process.
* **False Positives in Sanctions/PEP Screening:** Common business or owner names trigger high volumes of false matches against PEP (Politically Exposed Persons) or sanctions watchlists. If fuzzy-matching rules are poorly configured, every false positive lands in a manual queue for human review.

### 3. Misalignment Between the Platform and Sponsor Banks

* **Inflexible Sponsor Risk Policies:** Embedded finance platforms typically rely on underlying bank partners or BAAS (Banking-as-a-Service) providers to approve accounts. If the software platform’s risk appetite does not match the sponsor bank's strict compliance policies, high rates of legitimate applicants get rejected or flagged.
* **Lack of Data Reuse:** If a business customer has already verified their business to use the platform's core SaaS tool, many platforms fail to reuse those verified records, forcing the customer to re-enter basic legal data for financial features.

### 4. Cross-Border & Data Registry Fragility

* **Fragmented Official Registries:** Public company registries differ wildly by state and country. While the UK’s Companies House offers accessible digital APIs, registry access across US state filing portals or EU jurisdictions can be fragmented, slow, or offline.
* **Complex Ownership Hierarchies:** When applicant companies are owned by parent corporations, holding entities, or offshore trusts, automated tools often fail to resolve the ownership tree automatically, forcing the applicant to provide custom ownership charts.

### 5. One-Size-Fits-All Verification Paths

* **Treating Low-Risk and High-Risk Entities Equally:** Routing a simple sole proprietor or local LLC through the exact same heavy Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) path as a complex, international enterprise leads to unnecessary friction. Failing to use early automated risk-scoring to streamline low-risk applications bogs down the entire onboarding pipeline.

---

- Compliance launched after product-market fit, leaving onboarding, monitoring, case management, and reporting disconnected. [arthatech](https://arthatech.net/blog/embedded-finance-compliance-how-to-scale-without-regulatory-risk/)

A resilient flow verifies the entity, resolves the UBO/control-person chain, screens all relevant parties, validates business purpose and expected activity, and produces a clear decision with an auditable reason. It should distinguish between an automatic approval, a request for specific documents, and a true decline—rather than sending every exception into a black-box review queue. exact_query: why do embedded finance platforms fail kyb onboarding
raw_response:
Embedded finance platforms fail KYB (Know Your Business) onboarding because verifying a business is significantly more complicated than verifying an individual.

An embedded finance platform may onboard thousands of businesses, merchants, suppliers, or marketplace sellers across multiple countries. Each business has different ownership structures, registration requirements, regulatory obligations, and risk profiles.

The core problem: KYB processes struggle to verify business identity, ownership, legitimacy, and risk quickly enough without creating friction for legitimate businesses.

## 1. The 8 main reasons embedded finance platforms fail KYB onboarding

### 1. Incomplete or inconsistent business information

Businesses submit information that doesn't match official records.

- Incorrect legal business names.
- Mismatched registration numbers.
- Outdated registered addresses.
- Incorrect tax identification numbers.
- Different information across application documents.

Why it happens: Businesses often operate with different trading names, legal names, and registered addresses.

Impact: Applications are rejected, flagged, or sent for manual review.

### 2. Complex ownership structures

KYB requires identifying the Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBOs) behind a business.

Common problems include:

- Multiple layers of corporate ownership.
- Foreign shareholders.
- Trusts and holding companies.
- Ownership spread across multiple individuals.
- Difficulty identifying individuals with significant control.

Why it happens: A platform may onboard a company whose ownership structure spans several jurisdictions.

Impact: The platform cannot confidently establish who ultimately owns or controls the business.

### 3. Missing or difficult-to-verify documentation

Platforms frequently request:

- Certificate of incorporation.
- Business registration documents.
- Proof of business address.
- Shareholder registers.
- Director identification.
- Ownership structure charts.
- Tax registration certificates.

Why it happens: Different countries issue different documents, in different formats and languages.

Impact: Onboarding gets stuck waiting for additional documentation.

### 4. Regulatory and compliance screening failures

Businesses and their associated individuals must be screened against relevant risk databases.

Typical issues include:

- Sanctions matches.
- Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs).
- Adverse media.
- High-risk business activities.
- Suspicious ownership connections.

Why it happens: Screening tools generate false positives, and businesses may share similar names with flagged entities.

Impact: Legitimate businesses get unnecessarily delayed while genuine risks require investigation.

### 5. Cross-border verification challenges

A business registered in one country may operate in another and have owners in several more.

For example:

- Company registered in the Netherlands.
- Founder based in Singapore.
- Shareholder registered in the British Virgin Islands.
- Customers located across Europe.

The platform must establish that the company exists, verify its ownership, and assess the relevant jurisdictional risks.

Impact: Inconsistent government registries, limited data availability, language barriers, and different regulatory requirements create onboarding friction.

### 6. Poor integration between KYB providers

Embedded finance platforms often rely on multiple third-party providers.

For example:

- Company registry verification provider.
- Identity verification provider.
- Sanctions screening provider.
- Document verification provider.
- Banking-as-a-Service (BaaS) partner.

Problems include:

- Different data formats.
- Inconsistent verification results.
- API downtime.
- Missing data fields.
- Poor communication between systems.

Impact: A business passes one verification step but fails another because the systems cannot reconcile their results.

### 7. Manual review bottlenecks

Some KYB cases cannot be approved automatically.

They require compliance analysts to:

- Review corporate documents.
- Investigate ownership structures.
- Resolve sanctions alerts.
- Request additional information.
- Make risk-based decisions.

Impact: Onboarding takes days or weeks instead of minutes or hours.

### 8. Banking partner risk appetite

This is particularly important in embedded finance.

An embedded finance platform may have its own onboarding policy, but its sponsor bank or regulated financial institution has separate risk requirements.

For example:

- The platform accepts a particular merchant category.
- The banking partner considers that category high-risk.
- The platform's KYB provider approves the company.
- The banking partner rejects the application.

Impact: A business passes the platform's KYB process but cannot access the financial product.

## 2. Where KYB onboarding breaks down

## Embedded finance KYB journey

1. Business application
   Failure: Incomplete forms, incorrect company information.
2. Business identity verification
   Failure: Unavailable registry records, mismatched registration details.
3. UBO and ownership verification
   Failure: Complex ownership structures, unidentified beneficial owners.
4. Document verification
   Failure: Missing, expired, inconsistent or unverifiable documents.
5. AML and risk screening
   Failure: Sanctions matches, PEP alerts, adverse media.
6. Banking partner approval
   Failure: Risk appetite mismatch or additional compliance requirements.
7. Account activation
   Failure: Technical integration issues or incomplete approval status.

## 3. Business impact of KYB onboarding failures

| Stakeholder | Business impact |
| --- | --- |
| Embedded finance platform | Lost customers and revenue |
| Merchant / SME | Delayed access to financial services |
| Banking partner | Increased compliance exposure |
| Compliance team | Higher manual review costs |
| KYB provider | Lower approval rates and customer dissatisfaction |
| Marketplace | Reduced merchant activation |

## 4. How can embedded finance platforms reduce KYB failures?

| Problem | Potential solution |
| --- | --- |
| Incorrect company information | Automated company registry validation |
| Complex ownership | Automated UBO identification and ownership mapping |
| Missing documents | Dynamic document collection |
| False-positive screening | Better alert matching and human review |
| Cross-border verification | Multi-jurisdictional KYB coverage |
| Provider integration issues | Unified KYB orchestration API |
| Manual review bottlenecks | Risk-based automated decisioning |
| Banking partner rejection | Predefined partner-specific risk rules |

## 5. The most important distinction: KYB rejection vs KYB abandonment

These are two different problems.

KYB rejectionThe business fails verification.

- Ownership cannot be verified.
- Compliance risk is identified.
- Documents are invalid.
- Banking partner declines.

KYB abandonmentThe business gives up before completion.

- Too many documents requested.
- Onboarding takes too long.
- Poor user experience.
- Repeated information requests.

This distinction matters because improving verification accuracy does not necessarily improve onboarding completion.

A platform can have excellent fraud detection but still lose legitimate customers because its onboarding experience is too complicated.

## 6\. The biggest business opportunity

There are three potential problems worth solving in the embedded finance market:

1\. KYB orchestration: One integration that connects multiple company registries, identity providers, document verification systems, and screening providers.

2\. KYB automation: Automatically extracting company information, mapping ownership structures, validating documents, and reducing manual reviews.

3\. KYB portability: Allowing verified business information to be reused across multiple financial institutions and embedded finance platforms, subject to consent, regulatory requirements, and freshness checks.

The third opportunity is particularly interesting because businesses often have to repeat similar KYB processes when onboarding with different financial providers.

## 7\. Key metrics to measure the problem

| Metric | What it measures |

exact_query: which payment providers support sepa instant payouts via api
raw_response:
Several payment providers, Banking-as-a-Service (BaaS) platforms, and clearing providers offer API access for **SEPA Instant Credit Transfers (SCT Inst)**. Under the EU Instant Payments Regulation, SEPA Instant allows euro payouts to land in destination bank accounts within seconds, 24/7/365.

Providers supporting automated SEPA Instant payouts via API are grouped by their core architecture and primary use cases below:

---

### 1. Payment Service Providers & Payment Gateways

Best for platforms, marketplaces, SaaS, and e-commerce merchants needing out-of-the-box merchant payout infrastructure.

* **Stripe (Connect & Payouts API):** Automatically routes eligible euro payouts through SEPA Instant when configured via the Payouts API or Stripe Connect dashboard. If a recipient bank doesn't support SEPA Instant, it gracefully falls back to standard SEPA Credit.
* **Adyen:** Offers real-time SEPA Instant payouts through its Payout API. Ideal for enterprise platforms needing fast, automated payout processing directly to bank accounts across the eurozone.
* **Mollie (Outbound Payments API):** Features a dedicated Outbound Payments API designed specifically for instant SEPA payouts. It processes payouts in under 10 seconds and includes automated **Verification of Payee (VOP)** to match IBANs with beneficiary names before initiating the payout.

---

### 2. Banking-as-a-Service (BaaS) & Embedded Finance Platforms

Best for fintechs, marketplaces, and platforms requiring dedicated virtual IBANs, multi-currency accounts, and programmatically managed wallet layers.

* **Swan:** Offers modern REST APIs enabling instant SEPA transfers out of European virtual IBAN accounts. If the receiving bank supports SCT Inst, Swan defaults to instant settlement within seconds.
* **Modulr:** Provides real-time payout capabilities with automatic failovers. Modulr attempts SEPA Instant first; if the beneficiary bank does not support instant transfers or encounters a temporary routing issue, the API can automatically retry or convert the payment into a standard SEPA Credit Transfer.
* **Mangopay:** Built for European marketplaces and crowdfunding platforms. Supports automated payouts via SEPA Instant from its multi-tenant wallet infrastructure.
* **FinXP:** Features dedicated BaaS APIs for euro account issuing and SEPA Instant payouts, reducing reliance on traditional correspondent banks.

---

### 3. Dedicated Mass Payout Engines & Cross-Border Rails

Best for companies managing high-volume worker payouts, creator payouts, platform gig payouts, or cross-border treasury movements.

* **Nium:** Offers real-time local clearing access across the EU via its unified Global Payout API, executing SEPA Instant transfers for euro payouts.
* **Revolut Business (Business API):** Allows businesses to integrate programmatic payouts. Euro transfers to SEPA Instant-compatible accounts settle in near real-time.
* **Tipalti:** Designed for mass B2B payouts, gig economy payouts, and supplier bills. Automates payout routing and executes real-time transfers via SEPA Instant where available.

---

### 4. Direct Clearing & Financial Infrastructure API Providers

Best for regulated financial institutions, Electronic Money Institutions (EMIs), and scale-up fintechs requiring direct access to clearing rails without intermediary markup.

* **ClearBank:** An API-first bank providing indirect connectivity to the SEPA scheme, enabling regulated institutions to programmatically send and receive SEPA Instant transfers.
* **Form3:** Cloud-native payment technology provider that connects banks and EMIs directly to SEPA Instant (TIPS / RT1 clearing engines) via a single API.

---

### Key Technical Considerations for SEPA Instant Payout APIs

| Consideration | Details |
| --- | --- |
| **Verification of Payee (VoP)** | Most modern payout APIs now include or mandate VoP checks via API to prevent misdirected payouts by confirming the name on the account matches the IBAN. |
| **Fallback Handling** | Ensure your API integration handles fallback logic (e.g., automatically routing via standard SEPA Credit if the destination bank rejects or does not support SEPA Instant). |
| **Transaction Limits** | While the traditional scheme cap was €100,000, individual providers set custom operational caps (e.g., Modulr supports outbound SEPA Instant up to higher operational limits). |
| **Webhooks & Status Updates** | Because SEPA Instant settles in seconds, look for providers that return synchronous transaction confirmations or immediate webhooks (`payment.processed` / `payment.failed`). |

exact_query: what licence does a fintech need to offer embedded payments in the eu
raw_response:
To offer embedded payments in the European Union (EU), a fintech’s regulatory licensing path depends entirely on whether it wants to **hold its own license** or **outsource regulated money handling to a partner**.

Under EU payment law (governed by PSD2 and the unified **PSD3/PSR framework**), any entity that touches customer funds, executes payment transactions, or initiates payments requires authorization.

---

### Path 1: "Unlicensed" Models (Outsourcing to a Partner)

Most fintech startups, SaaS companies, and marketplaces launch embedded payments without directly applying for an EU payment license. Instead, they choose one of three regulatory structures:

#### A. Embedded BaaS / PSP Partner Model (Most Common)

* **How it Works:** The fintech acts as the **front-end software layer** while a fully licensed Payment Service Provider (PSP) or Banking-as-a-Service (BaaS) provider (e.g., Stripe Connect, Swan, Adyen, Modulr) handles all regulatory functions.
* **Who holds the license?** The partner holds the license; the fintech does not.
* **Fintech Responsibility:** Customer onboarding UX, product features, and first-line application handling.
* **Partner Responsibility:** Fund safeguarding, compliance/KYB/KYC checks, regulatory reporting, and actual fund settlement.

#### B. Payment Agent / Distributor Model

* **How it Works:** The fintech formally registers as an **Agent** or **Distributor** of a licensed EU Payment Institution or EMI.
* **Requirements:** The partner PSP submits an application to its home financial regulator (e.g., BaFin, ACPR, DNB, CSSF) to register the fintech.
* **Fintech Responsibility:** The fintech can market and distribute payment services directly under the partner's regulatory umbrella, but must strictly adhere to the partner’s compliance policies and oversight.

#### C. Commercial Agent Exemption (Shrinking Option)

* **Historical Context:** Platforms previously tried using the "commercial agent exemption" under PSD2 to handle buyer/seller funds without a license.
* **Current Status under PSD3/PSR:** EU regulators have restricted this exemption. It only applies if the platform acts *exclusively* for either the buyer or the seller (not both) and has genuine authority to negotiate terms. Handling funds as a standard multi-vendor marketplace now requires a partner or a license.

---

### Path 2: Obtaining a Direct EU License

If a fintech wants to handle funds directly, manage internal ledgers, or capture higher payment margins without a BaaS middleman, it must apply for a license from a National Competent Authority (NCA) in an EU member state.

#### 1. Payment Institution (PI) License

* **Best For:** Merchants, payment gateways, and acquiring platforms processing transfers, card payments, or pay-by-bank features without issuing electronic wallets.
* **Key Features:** Allows executing payment transactions, issuing payment instruments, acquiring payments, and operating Payment Initiation Services (PISP).
* **Capital Requirement:** €125,000 initial capital for standard payment services.
* **Fund Rules:** Funds cannot sit indefinitely on the PI's balance sheet and must be safeguarded in segregated bank accounts or insurance policies.

#### 2. Electronic Money Institution (EMI) License

* **Best For:** Fintechs offering digital wallets, stored-value accounts, pre-paid corporate cards, or issuing virtual IBANs to store customer funds.
* **Key Features:** Includes all PI capabilities plus the legal right to issue **electronic money (e-money)**.
* **Capital Requirement:** €350,000 initial capital.
* **Fund Rules:** Must safeguard e-money 1:1 with fiat currency. Cannot pay interest on user balances or provide general credit/lending.

*(Note: Under **PSD3**, the EU is consolidating the PI and EMI licensing framework into a **single Payment Institution framework** with unified authorization rules, though e-money activity will remain a specific sub-category).*

#### 3. Credit Institution (Full Banking License)

* **Best For:** Platforms offering full deposit-taking, interest-bearing business accounts, overdrafts, and balance-sheet lending.
* **Requirements:** €5M+ initial capital, 2–4 years for regulatory approval, and heavy ongoing prudential reporting under ECB/national supervision.

---

### Overview of Licensing Paths

| Regulatory Path | Initial Capital Required | Time to Market | Who Safeguards Client Funds? | Direct Passporting Rights across 30 EU/EEA Countries? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **BaaS / PSP Partner** | €0 (Software setup costs) | Weeks to 3 Months | The BaaS / PSP Partner | N/A (Handled via Partner) |
| **Registered Agent** | €0 (Under partner license) | 2 to 6 Months | The Principal PI/EMI | Yes (Via Principal's notification) |
| **Payment Institution (PI)** | €125,000 | 9 to 18 Months | Safeguarded at a partner bank | **Yes** (Direct EU Passport) |
| **E-Money Institution (EMI)** | €350,000 | 12 to 24 Months | Safeguarded 1:1 at partner banks | **Yes** (Direct EU Passport) |
| **Full Bank License** | €5,000,000+ | 2 to 4 Years | On bank's balance sheet (covered by DGS) | **Yes** (Direct EU Passport) |

If it merely refers customers to or integrates a regulated provider, it may need no payment licence; if it executes payments, holds customer funds, issues e-money, or issues cards, it needs either its own authorisation or to operate under a licensed partner. ## Licence by activity

| Embedded-payment activity | Typical requirement |
|---|---|
| Referring users to a PSP, displaying payment options, or integrating a provider’s checkout | Usually no PI/EMI licence, provided the fintech does not execute payment services or hold funds.  [wallester](https://wallester.com/blog/our-products/embedded-finance/card-issuing-licence-and-payment-compliance-for-embedded-cards) |
| Accepting card payments on behalf of merchants | A **Payment Institution (PI)** licence, or use of a licensed acquirer/PSP.  [coredo](https://coredo.eu/licences/financial/psp/) |
| Money remittance, transfers, payment initiation, or account information | A **PI** licence, unless using a licensed provider.  [wallester](https://wallester.com/blog/our-products/embedded-finance/card-issuing-licence-and-payment-compliance-for-embedded-cards) |
| Holding a customer balance that can be spent later, issuing wallets, or issuing prepaid/debit cards funded by that balance | An **Electronic Money Institution (EMI)** licence, or an arrangement with a licensed EMI.  [wallester](https://wallester.com/blog/our-products/embedded-finance/card-issuing-licence-and-payment-compliance-for-embedded-cards) |
| Holding customer deposits and offering banking services | A **credit institution / banking licence**, not merely an EMI.  [wallester](https://wallester.com/blog/our-products/embedded-finance/card-issuing-licence-and-payment-compliance-for-embedded-cards) |
| Issuing cards without holding balances | May be possible through a BIN sponsor or programme manager; the fintech may not itself be the regulated issuer.  [wallester](https://wallester.com/blog/our-products/embedded-finance/card-issuing-licence-and-payment-compliance-for-embedded-cards) |

## The two main licences

### Payment Institution (PI)

A PI licence covers regulated payment services such as payment execution, money remittance, acquiring, payment initiation, and account information services. It does **not** allow the firm to issue e-money or hold customer stored value. [wallester](https://wallester.com/blog/our-products/embedded-finance/card-issuing-licence-and-payment-compliance-for-embedded-cards)

This is generally the right licence for a payment gateway, remittance product, or platform that processes transactions for merchants but does not maintain spendable customer balances. [coredo](https://coredo.eu/licences/financial/psp/)

### Electronic Money Institution (EMI)

An EMI licence permits the firm to issue e-money, maintain stored value, and provide payment services. It is the standard route for embedded wallets, prepaid or debit cards linked to a balance, and marketplace models where funds are held before release to a seller. [wallester](https://wallester.com/blog/our-products/embedded-finance/card-issuing-licence-and-payment-compliance-for-embedded-cards)

For example, a marketplace that lets buyers pay now and releases funds to sellers after delivery may need EMI-level capability if it holds customer funds in e-money; otherwise, it may rely on a licensed EMI or payment provider to provide that infrastructure. [wallester](https://wallester.com/blog/our-products/embedded-finance/card-issuing-licence-and-payment-compliance-for-embedded-cards)

## EU licensing mechanics

There is no single “EU fintech licence.” A fintech obtains authorisation from the **national competent authority** in one EU member state, then can generally passport that authorisation across the EEA. [iclg](https://iclg.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/netherlands/)

In the Netherlands, for example, a firm providing payment services generally needs authorisation from De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB), unless an exemption applies. The application includes a programme of operations, business plan, budget forecast, and evidence of initial capital. [iclg](https://iclg.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/netherlands/)

## Practical routes to market

| Route | When it makes sense | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|

## 8. What licence does a fintech need to offer embedded payments in the EU?

A fintech generally needs a Payment Institution (PI) licence under PSD2 or an Electronic Money Institution (EMI) licence, depending on the payment services it intends to offer.

However, there is no single licence specifically for embedded payments. The regulatory requirement depends on how the fintech handles customer funds, initiates transactions and executes payments.

### 1. Main licensing options

| Licence / status | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| Payment Institution (PI) | Providing regulated payment services, such as executing payments, payment accounts and acquiring transactions. |
| Electronic Money Institution (EMI) | Issuing electronic money, holding customer funds in exchange for e-money and providing payment services. |
| Banking licence | Accepting deposits and providing banking and payment services within the scope of the authorisation. |
| No own licence – partner model | Offering payments through a licensed bank, PI or EMI, subject to the applicable outsourcing, agency and regulatory requirements. |

### 2. Which licence is needed for different embedded payment models?

- Payment acceptance and acquiring: A PI or EMI authorisation covering acquiring payment transactions, or a bank licence.
- Payment accounts and money transfers: Typically a PI or EMI authorisation covering the relevant payment services.
- Digital wallets and stored balances: Generally an EMI licence if the fintech issues electronic money.
- Payment initiation (Pay by Bank): Authorisation as a Payment Initiation Service Provider (PISP).
- Account information services: Registration as an Account Information Service Provider (AISP).
- Payment orchestration or technical infrastructure: Potentially no payment licence if the fintech strictly provides technical services without possessing funds or independently providing regulated payment services.

The distinction between a technical service provider and a regulated payment provider is particularly important. Calling a product a payment orchestration platform does not automatically remove licensing requirements.

### 3. Can a fintech offer embedded payments without obtaining its own licence?

Yes. A common approach is to partner with an already licensed PI, EMI or bank.

There are three typical structures:

1. White-label / Banking-as-a-Service model

- A licensed financial institution provides the regulated payment services.
- The fintech provides the user interface, technology and customer experience.
- The regulated partner remains responsible for the regulated activities allocated to it.

2. Registered agent model

- The fintech acts on behalf of an authorised PI or EMI.
- The agent must generally be registered with the relevant regulator before providing payment services.
- The licensed institution retains regulatory responsibility for the agent's activities.

3. Technical service provider model

- The fintech supplies software, APIs, payment routing or infrastructure.
- It does not itself perform regulated payment services or possess customer funds.
- The technical service provider exclusion under PSD2 may apply.

The agent and technical service provider models are not interchangeable: the actual activities and flow of funds determine the regulatory treatment.

### 4. What are the requirements for obtaining a PI or EMI licence?

Under the current EU framework, the main requirements include:

- Establishment of a legal entity in an EU Member State.
- Minimum initial capital, depending on the payment services offered.
- Fit-and-proper management and qualifying shareholders.
- Robust governance and internal controls.
- AML/KYC and transaction-monitoring arrangements.
- Safeguarding of customer funds.
- Operational resilience, cybersecurity and risk-management procedures.
- Appropriate outsourcing and third-party risk-management arrangements.
- A compliant business plan and financial forecasts.

An authorised PI or EMI can generally use EU passporting arrangements to provide permitted services in other EU Member States, subject to the applicable notification procedures.

### 5. What are the minimum capital requirements?

Under the current PSD2 and EMD2 framework:

| Licence | Minimum initial capital |
| --- | --- |
| PI – Payment initiation only | €20,000 |
| PI – Money remittance only | €50,000 |
| PI – Other core payment services, including acquiring | €125,000 |
| EMI – Electronic money institution | €350,000 |

These are initial capital thresholds, not the full ongoing own-funds requirements.

### 6. Which regulator supervises the fintech?

The fintech applies to the regulator in the EU Member State where it establishes its licensed entity.

For example, in the Netherlands:

- DNB (De Nederlandsche Bank): Authorises and supervises payment institutions and electronic money institutions.
- AFM (Authority for the Financial Markets): Has relevant responsibilities in financial markets and consumer protection.

A Dutch-authorised PI or EMI can potentially passport its permitted services across the EU.

### 7. Important regulatory development: PSD3 and PSR

As of November 2026, the EU is transitioning from PSD2 towards PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation (PSR).

A political agreement was reached in November 2025, and the Council adopted its negotiating position on 29 October 2026. The final legislative process and publication are still pending.

Fintechs planning to launch embedded payment products should therefore design their compliance frameworks with the forthcoming rules in mind. PSD2 remains the operative framework until the new legislation takes effect.

- Faster market entry: Partner with an existing licensed PI or EMI and operate through an appropriate technical service provider or registered agent arrangement.

The choice largely depends on whether the fintech wants to control the payment flow and customer funds itself.

The key question is: Does the fintech actually receive, hold, transfer or acquire customer funds, or does it simply provide the technology layer connecting merchants to a licensed payment provider?

That distinction often determines whether it needs its own licence.

| **FX Spread Markup** | **0.2% to 3.5%+** above interbank rate | **The largest hidden cost.** Most banks and processors add a markup above the live interbank exchange rate instead of charging a transparent fee. |
| **Correspondent / SWIFT Fees** | **$15 to $50** per transfer | Intermediary banks deduct processing fees along the SWIFT chain (unless sent via OUR instructions or local clearing rails). |
| **Cross-Border Card Surcharges** | **1.0% to 2.0%** additional | If paying B2B invoices via commercial credit cards, Visa/Mastercard apply international card surcharges and cross-border assessment fees. |

| Method | Estimated all-in cost | Recipient receives |

These are illustrative, corridor-dependent estimates. A bank wire may also charge a fixed outgoing fee—often around $40 or more—plus intermediary deductions and an FX spread. [xtransfer](https://www.xtransfer.com/us/blog/best-low-fee-b2b-payment-platforms)

## What drives the real cost

The headline fee is only one layer. Compare:

- **FX spread:** the gap between the interbank/mid-market rate and the rate you receive.
- **Outgoing transfer fee:** the provider’s fixed or percentage fee.
- **Intermediary-bank deductions:** fees removed by correspondent banks on SWIFT routes.
- **Receiving-bank charges:** fees deducted by the beneficiary bank.
- **Payout or beneficiary fees:** especially for marketplace payouts, cards, wallets, or cash pickup.
- **Account and minimum fees:** monthly platform fees, minimum volumes, and inactivity charges. [lumx](https://lumx.io/blog-posts/cross-border-payment-costs-2026)

For B2B payments globally, the Financial Stability Board’s average total cost is about **1.6%**, of which about **1.4 percentage points** is FX; roughly 87% of the total cost is therefore FX-related. [lumx](https://lumx.io/blog-posts/cross-border-payment-costs-2026)

## Best choice by corridor

- **EUR within SEPA:** Use SEPA Credit Transfer or, for eligible cases, SEPA Instant; costs should be low and often near-zero or fixed rather than percentage-based.
- **Major developed-market corridors:** **Wise Business** is often the most transparent benchmark, with roughly 0.41%–0.71% pricing. [xtransfer](https://www.xtransfer.com/us/blog/best-low-fee-b2b-payment-platforms)
- **China and high-volume trade corridors:** **XTransfer** can be highly competitive at 0.1%–0.4%, especially where local-rail settlement avoids SWIFT intermediaries. [xtransfer](https://www.xtransfer.com/us/blog/best-low-fee-b2b-payment-platforms)
- **Multi-currency operating model:** **Airwallex** is compelling when you need balances, FX conversion, and payments in one platform. [xtransfer](https://www.xtransfer.com/us/blog/best-low-fee-b2b-payment-platforms)
- **Marketplace payouts to many recipient types:** **Payoneer** or **Hyperwallet** are more relevant, but validate the cost per payout method. [xtransfer](https://www.xtransfer.com/us/blog/best-low-fee-b2b-payment-platforms)
- **Large invoices:** Do not default to cards; use bank rails, local transfers, or negotiated FX pricing. [paystand](https://www.paystand.com/blog/international-business-payments)

## How to compare quotes

Ask each provider for a **landed-cost quote** for a specific amount, currency pair, corridor, and settlement speed. Require the following in writing:

- Exact FX rate or spread versus mid-market.
- Outgoing transfer fee.
- Intermediary-bank fees, if any.
- Receiving-bank fees, if any.
- Whether the recipient receives the full quoted amount.
- Settlement time and cut-off times.
- Fees for returns, refunds, recalls, and failed payments. [lumx](https://lumx.io/blog-posts/cross-border-payment-costs-2026)

A useful rule: compare the **recipient’s net amount**, not the sender’s advertised fee. Two providers can charge the same “0.5%” but deliver materially different amounts after FX and intermediary deductions. [lumx](https://lumx.io/blog-posts/cross-border-payment-costs-2026)
